doc.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Plunger and derby technique learned with Ellington
summary: How to manipulate the plunger and derby mutes, 'how now brown cow'.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: I asked this a little bit different, when I asked you to go back again – did you learn anything as far as technique or in the jazz idiom in that band?

Oh sure. I learned, first of all, how to interpret Ellington’s music in the fashion that I knew he wanted it interpreted. I knew that in order to manipulate and articulate properly the plunger movements, you had to do it a certain way. You just couldn’t go in there and take a plunger, say “quack, quack, quack,” which is what most people do. You have to indulge in the total manipulation of the plunger. One thing that we teach in jazz education today, young people who are getting involved, we teach them to really articulate and manipulate the plunger with, in mind, one of the old English lessons: “how now brown cow.” All of these manipulations and movements of the plunger that get these effects – “now”: come from out, in. “O” would be marked as an open tone, and “+” would be closer to the bell. “goo gok goo gok gok gow.” Then you could use that in conjunction with a growl, or a burr, or a flutter-tongue [Terry vocalizes each one]. So you got “umm grr drrrrl,” all of them with manipulations of the plunger.

Derbies, the same thing, same thing. We got into – the Basie band was very notorious for that, and that’s a lost art today: how far in, how far out, and how far to swing the derby. [Terry vocalizes derby-muted effects.] You could bend notes with it. But it’s something that you have to do in order to be good at it.
